Ask a good doctor whether early screening saves lives, and the answer arrives fast: yes, obviously, catch the tumor small and you catch it in time. Every year I hear some version of this, and it has the ring of settled sense. The individual case is legible. A patient walks in, a scan finds a shadow, the shadow comes out, the patient walks home. What could be plainer? This is the humane view, the bedside view, and I will grant it its full force before I quarrel with anything. At the scale of one frightened person on one examining table, screening earlier is simply better medicine. That claim does real work, and I do not intend to insult it.

The trouble begins the moment you count. Screening a healthy population turns up findings that would never have troubled anyone—slow lesions, indolent growths, the biological equivalent of a rattle in an engine that will outlast the car. The rival framing, which the epidemiologists press hard, calls this overdiagnosis, and it sounds like the responsible position: treat fewer, harm fewer, spare the anxious biopsies. Notice that framing carefully, because it is not mine, though I will let it speak. Here is my claim, stated plainly: a benefit that is real for each patient can be unreal for the patients taken together. Screening does something for the person that it does not do for the population. The bedside verdict and the ledger verdict are both honest, and they point opposite ways.

Sharpen it. The benefit is not merely diluted at scale; it can reverse sign. A test that saves this man's life can, run across a million men, add more deaths from the treatments than it subtracts from the disease. Same intervention. Same logic. The arithmetic simply changes hands.

Now, the fair objection. Surely, someone says, this is just a technical problem—better tests, sharper thresholds, and the two scales snap back into agreement. Refine the tool and the individual good becomes the aggregate good, as it always should have been. I want to concede as much of this as I honestly can, because the impulse is right and much of medicine has improved exactly this way. Yes: some scale gaps are fixable, and pretending otherwise is lazy. But concede too much and you miss what the concession quietly surrenders. The technical fix assumes the two verdicts want to converge. My whole point is that they need not. The gap is not always noise waiting to be cleaned up. Sometimes it is the shape of the thing.

So sharpen once more, and surrender the comfort. The individual claim is true. The aggregate claim is true. They do not meet. There is no altitude from which both resolve, only a choice of which one you will act on today. I have spent a career signing off on protocols written for populations and then watching them applied, one body at a time, to people who are not populations. That is the vantage this whole argument was written from—the desk where the ledger lands and the patient waits. From there you learn the ugly thing early. Choosing the scale is not a preliminary to the decision. It is the decision. And nobody hands you the scale.

There is a species of literary piety that treats every translation as a small catastrophe, a leaking vessel from which meaning drips away between languages. Something is always lost, the saying goes, as if loss were the natural condition of the work rather than the alibi of the lazy. I have never trusted it. The word *translate* descends from the Latin *translatus*, the participle of *transferre*, to carry across; a load carried across a river need not spill. A competent porter delivers the crate intact. Most of what passes for untranslatability, on inspection, is simply a translator who has not yet found the right word.

The trouble is that the right word keeps refusing to exist. Take the German *gemütlich*, or the Portuguese *saudade*, or the way Homer's *polytropos* holds within one adjective both cunning and much-travelled — no single English coin carries the same weight, and the translator must strike a new one, choosing which face to show. Rhythm compounds the problem: a line that scans in the source falls flat rendered word for word, so the porter must repack the crate to make it balance. I concede this, reluctantly, because the examples give me no choice. What survives the concession, I told myself, is still a craft of approximation — skilled compromise, the disciplined narrowing of loss, the technician's art of getting as close as the two languages permit. The translator judges; but he judges toward a fixed target, and his judgments are corrections, not inventions.

Then one notices what the receiving language actually keeps. The King James renderings of the Psalms are studied as English literature; Fitzgerald's *Rubáiyát* outlived, in influence, the Persian quatrains it loosely quarried; Schlegel's Shakespeare became a German possession, read as German. These are not approximations that got unusually near their targets. They are new verbal artifacts with aesthetic lives their originals never predicted — objects that later writers imitate, that shape a literature's own sense of its cadences. The buried layer here is the old word *auctor*, from *augere*, to make grow, to originate. A translation that a tradition builds upon is not a copy shading toward its source; it originates. And once that is admitted, the technician's model collapses. The translator is not narrowing loss against a fixed target. He is authoring.

So I grant it: translation is authorship, and the porter was always a fiction. But an admission of this size arrives with an invoice, and the invoice falls due on a matter I had filed as trivial — the name on the spine. If the translator originates, then his name must carry an author's freight, an author's credit and an author's liability, printed as large and answered to as fully. That is the price, and it is steeper than it looks, because it revokes the reader's oldest comfort: the belief that in reading Tolstoy in English one is reading Tolstoy, unmediated, and not the second author whose invisibility was the whole condition of the illusion.

The reformers who spent the last century demanding that institutions open their books did not imagine themselves as utopians. Their premise was almost mechanical: concealment shelters incompetence and worse, and light disinfects. They borrowed their faith from a courtroom and a laboratory at once — testimony given in the open is harder to falsify, a specimen held to the light easier to judge. Against the closed committee, the sealed ledger, the decision reached by men whose reasons were never written down, they proposed one remedy: disclosure. Make the institution show its workings and the workings will improve, since no one behaves the same way watched as unwatched. It was a critique of power that took a curiously optical form, and for a long stretch it worked as advertised.

The victory is easy to read in the furniture of ordinary institutional life. Minutes are published, budgets posted, the audit and the records request now count as unremarkable fixtures rather than hard-won concessions. Whole professions grew up to service the expectation — compliance officers, disclosure counsel, the salaried officer whose very title is transparency. The demand became a norm and then a reflex; an agency that refused to publish today would seem not merely secretive but eccentric, a holdout against a settled expectation. Measured against its own stated aims, it is difficult to name a reform of the period that succeeded more thoroughly.

But a reflex is easy to feed. The institution obliged to disclose learns to disclose enormously — to meet the request for its reasons with ten thousand pages in which the reason, should it survive at all, drifts unmarked among procedural sediment. Nothing is concealed; nothing is locatable. Compliance by volume is still compliance, and it honours every letter of the rule while quietly draining the rule of its point.

The error, if there was one, lay in measuring the reform along the wrong axis. The question was never how much an institution reveals but in which direction the seeing runs. A posted budget makes the institution faintly legible to a citizen with no time to read it; that same institution, across the same years, learned to read the citizen with increasing exactness — his filings, his purchases, his movements composed into a profile far more usable than any minutes he might retrieve. Disclosure travelled one way and legibility the other, and the two were never equal quantities. The room did not open so much as turn: the glass that once shielded the institution from view now faces inward, and the citizen stands on its lit side.

So the question worth keeping is not whether the institution has been compelled to show itself. That contest is settled, and its settlement altered almost nothing about the arrangement that mattered. The reformers won the argument they were having; they did not notice the argument moving. The question is who, within the arrangement, has been rendered readable to whom, and at what resolution — a budget posted where no one can parse it and a dossier assembled where its subject will never see it are not opposite conditions but one asymmetry, reported from either end.

Ask a chess grandmaster why she sacrificed the knight, and she will tell you a story. She saw the weakness on the long diagonal; she judged the initiative worth a piece; she trusted her opponent to flinch. It is a lovely story, and I have no wish to spoil the dinner by doubting it. The trouble is that the story explains too much and predicts too little. Give me a hundred grandmasters and a hundred such positions and I will show you the sacrifice appearing at roughly the same rate whether or not any particular player consulted the long diagonal at all. The reasons people offer are sincere, various, and beautifully articulated, and they float above the regularity like the smell of good cooking above a kitchen that would produce the same meal without it. I am not saying the players are lying. I am saying their reasons are a running commentary on a game whose moves were already constrained by the board. We reach, understandably, for the agent — the deliberating, choosing, reason-giving self — because that is who we can interview. The interview is charming. It is also, I suspect, the least reliable witness in the building, precisely because it is the one that always has something to say.

So perhaps the thing to explain is not the chooser but the distribution of choices. Drop the interview. Watch the pattern instead.

Consider markets. Consider queues. Consider birds. Prices settle. Lines find their length. Flocks bank as one. No bird decides the turn. Each obeys three dull local rules, and the elegance is the sum. The equilibrium needs no author. It needs only agents too simple to have a story.

And here the neat picture buckles, which is the interesting part. For the equilibrium account, having banished the deliberating chooser, quietly smuggles back a chooser of its own — the system — and grants it exactly the coherence it denied the individual. The flock does not deliberate, true. But when I say the market "finds" a price or the queue "seeks" its length, I have not eliminated purpose; I have relocated it, from the visible agent I could interrogate to an invisible one I cannot. That is a strange trade for a skeptic to make. The local rule was innocent. The global claim is not, because the local rules were never asked to add up to a thing that wants. What the agency-talk loses is real: it treats the running commentary as the cause, and mistakes fluency for control. What the systems-talk cannot see is also real: at the level where the pattern lives, the deliberating self has vanished entirely, and with it any account of the one moment that will not average out — the move no distribution predicted, made by a player who, this once, meant it. Neither picture holds that moment. Both explain around it. I may be missing something, but I do not think either of them is looking where it fell.

A concert of Persian classical song ends, and the listeners filing out do not ask whether the singer was skilled. They ask whether hāl came. The word is Sufi in ancestry and common in Tehran green rooms; it names whatever makes one evening an event and another, note for note its equal, a recital. At home the word works without friction. Trouble begins at the border, when a critic writing in English reaches for an equivalent and finds the shelves stocked with the wrong kind of goods.

The first consignment offered in exchange: "atmosphere," "mood," "presence." Each is a property word. Where the London reviewer writes that a performance possessed presence, the Tehran listener says that hāl arrived — and the grammar is the tell. Properties are possessed; hāl visits. A property belongs to the performance and can be praised in the singer's absence; hāl is said to come, to descend, occasionally to refuse. Property words travel well precisely because they fasten to objects, and objects can be shipped. What hāl names spoils in transit, like fruit picked for a market it will never reach.

The laboratory tradition makes the second attempt. "Flow" — the psychologist's term for absorbed, self-forgetting performance — at least treats an occurrence rather than a thing. But flow is filed under the performer's mind, and hāl declines the filing: veterans of the repertoire insist it can desert a technically flawless night and descend, unearned, on a singer whose voice is breaking. It seems to belong to the room, if it belongs anywhere. So the deadlock: one customs house registers the evening under the work, the other under the psyche. Neither ledger has a column for what the listeners were pointing at.

A third tradition breaks the tie. Sanskrit poetics built its edifice on rasa — "taste," "savour" — and its theorists spent centuries insisting, against exactly these two filings, that rasa resides neither in the dramatic work nor in the spectator's private feeling but in the tasting itself, an event requiring both and reducible to neither. Two traditions with no common ancestor arriving at the same refusal suggest the refusal is load-bearing. The resistance of hāl to translation is not a lexical gap awaiting a cleverer dictionary; it marks a disagreement about where aesthetic value lives. A critical vocabulary is an inventory of locations, and the inventory English criticism inherited was drawn up for goods that hold still: the painting, the printed poem. Performance got appraised with instruments calibrated for objects.

None of this convicts property-criticism of error on its own ground; for the things that hold still, it holds. The verdict is narrower and firmer: judgment of performance, in any tradition, needs terms for events, and borrowing object-terms smuggles in a metaphysics along with the vocabulary. Until reviewing learns to grade evenings rather than works, hāl will stay where it is. Some words refuse the crossing not because the road is poor but because what they name has no address on the far side.

The question was answered a long time ago, and answered well. Free will is a confusion. This is not the shrill verdict of a partisan; it is the calm settlement of a field that has done its due diligence, weighed the alternatives with unusual patience, and found only one survivor. The libertarian's uncaused cause was inspected and found to be a superstition wearing a lab coat. The compatibilist's rescue—will is freedom from constraint, not from causation—was tested against ordinary usage and held. Determinism absorbed the rest. Even the holdouts concede the machinery: neurons fire on schedule, and the schedule does not consult us. Every serious survey confirms the drift. The textbooks agree. The philosophers of mind agree, more or less, in the way people agree who no longer expect to be surprised. What remains is bookkeeping. One tidies the vocabulary, retires the theological residue, and moves on to problems with a pulse. The matter is closed. The clock, so to speak, has been opened, and the movement inside runs exactly as predicted.

How did it close? Not by a single proof but by a slow attrition of opponents. Each generation inherited the previous generation's exhaustion. The libertarian position grew tiresome to defend, so fewer defended it; fewer defenders meant weaker defense, which confirmed the weakness. There is a bolder reading available, and it has adherents: that the debate was never about metaphysics at all, only about which words we are permitted to keep. On this view the whole quarrel dissolves into grammar, and the winner is simply whoever last controlled the dictionary. Tidy. It has the appeal of every position that mistakes its own confidence for depth.

Notice what the attrition selected for. Not truth—stamina. A verdict reached by the exhaustion of dissent records who tired first, not who was right. The consensus is a fact about the debaters, not about the will. This is the delayed referent: the "due diligence" of the opening was never diligence about free will; it was diligence about maintaining agreement. A field can be scrupulous about its manners and careless about its object. The machinery ran as predicted because it was built to. That is watchmaking, not discovery.

So the tempting middle is refused. One could say the question is answered *and* the process was flawed, and split the difference. No. A conclusion certified by fatigue is not half-earned; it is uncertified. Whether free will survives inspection remains genuinely open, precisely because the inspection never happened. The clock keeps time. Nobody checked it against the sun.

Ask a psycholinguist how long it takes to find a word and a number comes back: some six hundred milliseconds from seeing a picture of a dog to saying "dog." The number is not invented. It is measured, replicated, sensitive to how common the word is and how recently it was last used. And it answers a question that, examined closely, was asking after something that is not there.

The picture behind the number is a warehouse. Words sit on shelves; a signal goes out; the right item is located, pulled, delivered to the mouth. "Retrieval" is the standard term, and it is a fetching word. On this picture finding takes time because searching takes time, and the six hundred milliseconds is the length of the errand. The tip-of-the-tongue state seems to clinch it: there sits the word, on its shelf, and the clerk cannot reach it. What could be more plainly an object temporarily out of reach?

Watch those milliseconds and the shelf is not there to be found. From the first instant dozens of words are partly active at once — the near-synonyms, the words that merely sound alike, the word in the other language a bilingual keeps. Nothing sits still awaiting collection; a field of candidates rises and falls together, each inhibiting the rest, until one settles out. The mistake was never in the stopwatch. It was in the noun. There is no located item and no act of locating; the question "how long to find the word" presupposes a thing found and a moment of finding, and neither survives the look.

This is easy to over-read, and the over-reading is tempting: if no word is fetched, then perhaps nothing is stored and knowing a language is some formless flux. That does not follow, and the field's own data forbid it. Frequency effects, neighbourhood effects, the sheer lawfulness of the errors — a speaker's knowledge has structure, and the structure governs what settles. What crosses the winning threshold must cross it before the mouth moves; that much is necessary. But a candidate's crossing is not the sufficient event the warehouse promised, a single retrieval datable to the millisecond. The crossing is the last ripple of a settling that had no single seat and no starting gun.

What remains, once the warehouse is emptied, is not nothing. The reaction times remain, and they still track difficulty. The errors remain, and they still betray structure. What dissolves is the errand and its object — the stored word, the search, the moment of arrival — and what stands in their place is humbler and less tractable: a settling with no address, clocked all along by an instrument that was timing something other than a journey.

The prevailing therapeutic sensibility of modern life rests on an unstated metaphysics: that the self is a durable substance which loss may bruise but cannot annihilate. Grief, on this view, is a temporary distortion of an intact core, and the proper response to the grieving is compassionate management—a gentle steering back toward the norm of wellbeing. The consoling scripts we offer the bereaved ("you have your whole life ahead of you," "time heals") are less expressions of recognition than instruments of correction. Embedded within them is the assumption that recovery is both possible and obligatory, that the sufferer is misreporting her own condition, exaggerating a wound that will, in time, close over the unbroken person beneath.

Yet certain testimonies resist this framework so stubbornly that they force a reconsideration of it. When a war widow says "I died the day he was killed," we instinctively hear a figure of speech, a hyperbole of mourning. But suppose the statement were treated not as symptom but as report. It would then contradict a lineage of thought—shared by Freudian psychoanalysis and ordinary common sense alike—according to which the self persists as long as biological life does, damaged perhaps, but fundamentally restorable. Freud believed that beneath trauma one could locate a self capable of repair. The philosopher Catherine Malabou proposes the opposite: what she terms *destructive plasticity*, a form of change that does not reshape identity but abolishes it, so that a genuinely new self emerges in the ruins of the old. On this account the person who declares her own death is not distorting reality; she is disclosing it.

The consequences are considerable. If we grant the traumatised the authority to report their own condition truthfully, the entire order of truth and distortion inverts. The therapeutic apparatus, with its diagnoses and protocols of healing, ceases to be the road to clarity and becomes instead the mechanism that obscures it. The widow, formerly a deviation from how a life ought to unfold, becomes a witness to the hidden structure of existence: that the self is not autonomous but relational, formed through bonds whose severance can genuinely undo it. To love another is thus to entrust part of one's life to that person's mortality—to accept the risk of dying several times across a lifetime.

This is not, however, an invitation to romanticise suffering as privileged access to sacred knowledge. What the moment of trauma discloses is precisely the *collapse* of meaning—the point at which language loses its purchase. The initiation it offers is an initiation into limit, not illumination. And here the argument must qualify itself: to say pain reveals a truth is not to say it should be sought, nor that every grieving person becomes a seer. The claim is narrower and harder—that the therapeutic wish to eliminate such pain may amount to a refusal to see what it exposes: that loss is the condition of connection, not an accident befalling it.

When Sartre insisted in 1945 that "existence precedes essence," he meant to overturn a hierarchy older than philosophy itself: the assumption that human beings arrive with a purpose already stitched into them, waiting only to be realized. On his account, we are first thrown into being and only afterward, through the accumulation of choices, become anything at all. The doctrine is exhilarating in its austerity. It abolishes excuses, dignifies the trembling moment of decision, and hands each person the full weight of authorship over a life. Yet the very radicalism that made the lecture resonate in a Paris still smelling of liberation is also where its architecture begins to buckle.

Consider the move that Sartre treats as the linchpin of his ethics. Having stripped away God, human nature, and any pre-given values, he still wants to prevent his philosophy from collapsing into "anything goes." His device is a peculiar universalizing gesture: in choosing for myself, I choose "as if" I were legislating for all humanity, and this imagined constituency supposedly disciplines my will. But the gesture is borrowed. It is Kant's categorical imperative wearing existentialist clothing, and it sits awkwardly on a thinker who has just denied that humans share any common essence. If there is no shared nature, there is no shared standard by which my choice could be a model for anyone else. The egomaniac who authentically wills his own aggrandizement, and who cheerfully invites everyone to do likewise, passes Sartre's test as easily as the saint. Authenticity certifies the sincerity of a choice; it says nothing about its content.

This is not a minor lacuna. It reveals that Sartre's ethics smuggles in the very universality it claims to have earned from within. Simone de Beauvoir, writing two years later, saw the gap and refused the smuggling. Her wager in *The Ethics of Ambiguity* is that freedom is never abstract but always *situated* — lived by particular people under particular constraints of poverty, oppression, and denied education. For her, the obligation to others' freedom is not imported through a Kantian back door; it follows necessarily from taking seriously that my own freedom is exercised in conditions that others' choices have shaped, and that shape theirs. Where Sartre gestures thinly at "situation," Beauvoir insists on the concrete social architecture within which the anguish of choice is sometimes swallowed whole by the anguish of survival.

The difference is not merely emphasis. Sartre's version can be read, and has been read, as a self-help creed: seize your life, defy the categories others impose, remake yourself. That reading is not wrong, but it is incomplete, because it treats the chooser as unencumbered. Beauvoir's correction returns the body and the world to the picture. Willing one's own freedom, she argues, commits one to fighting for the conditions that make anyone else's freedom possible. Freedom that ignores its own conditions is, in the end, less a philosophy than a flattering wish.

Anthropologists who study expertise have been arguing about the same thing for forty years, and the argument has the stability of a well-set trap. On one side, the apprenticeship school: expert skill is tacit, lodged in the trained body, learned by standing beside a master and absorbing what no manual records. On the other, the codification school: what looks ineffable is only unarticulated rule, latent structure the expert follows without being able to recite, and patient study can write it down. The witnesses are distinguished, the fieldwork on both sides is real, and the verdict never comes.

Examine the exhibits and a pattern emerges that should trouble both counsel. The apprenticeship school's best evidence is the residue: whenever a craft is reduced to protocol, something escapes, and the seasoned practitioner still outperforms the fully instructed novice. The codification school's best evidence is the history of that residue — that yesterday's unteachable knack becomes today's checklist, the ineffable shrinking under study. Neither side notices that these are the same fact told twice. A residue that is always present and always diminishing is exactly what each school requires: it hands the first its mystery and the second its progress, in perpetuity. The dispute does not persist despite the evidence. It persists because the evidence was built to feed both mouths.

The reason the trap holds is a premise the two schools share and neither inspects: that expertise is a possession, something an individual has, the only question being where inside the expert it sits — in the hand or in an unspoken rulebook. Set that premise beside the fieldwork and it wobbles. The diagnostician who is unmistakably expert in her own clinic becomes a merely careful stranger when she locums across town; the skill that seemed to travel in her body stayed behind with her instruments, her colleagues, her nurses' half-second glances, the deference of patients who knew her name. Expertise in these records is less a thing carried than a standing conferred, assembled at a site and dismantled when the site changes. If that is right, the residue and the checklist are both taking inventory of a warehouse that was never where the goods were kept.

This is not a ruling for the relational account. That the container premise wobbles is not proof that expertise is nothing but arrangement, and the ethnographies that would decide it have not been done. The point is narrower and less convenient: the standing dispute cannot be settled from within, because both parties are underwritten by the assumption whose abandonment any settlement requires, and each is professionally built on it — the romantics of the workshop and the engineers of the protocol alike need the expert to be a container. Until one of them consents to empty it, the case cannot close. The ledger stays open, its two columns balanced against each other and neither against the world.

Consider a young woman from a neighborhood where the local high school's graduation rate hovers below fifty percent. She wins a scholarship to a selective preparatory academy, and once there she studies with a discipline that her teachers describe, without exaggeration, as unusual: four hours of homework nightly, weekends surrendered to problem sets, summers spent finishing coursework other students had abandoned. She graduates first in her cohort and matriculates at an elite university. The story, told this way, arrives pre-packaged with its own moral: talent plus effort overcomes disadvantage, and the rest of us should take note.

Granted, she did do the work no one else was willing to do. But the scholarship she used to enter that academy existed only because a wealthy alumnus, prompted by his own child's teacher to fund "deserving cases," had endowed it two decades earlier. Her opportunity was itself the residue of somebody else's money and somebody else's judgment about who deserved it.

Return again to her trajectory and a further layer surfaces. Her capacity for those four-hour nightly sessions depended on her mother's shift schedule, which happened to allow evenings at home rather than a second job; on a tutoring program at the academy funded by other parents' donations, open to her only because she'd been admitted at all; and on the simple absence of any obligation to earn wages herself, an absence not shared by several of her more exhausted classmates. The discipline was hers. Its preconditions were not distributed at random.

None of this cancels the other. She worked harder than most of her peers; that labor was real and specific, not a fiction laid over passivity. It was also assembled, plank by plank, from conditions she did not build and could not have built alone. The tidy story cracks here.

Now place her twenty years later, a hiring manager who credits her own success entirely to discipline and speaks of it, sincerely, as proof that merit finds a way. Reviewing résumés, she favors candidates who volunteered abroad, who speak in the cadences she recognizes, who mention the same handful of internships obtained through family friends — candidates, in short, who had the leisure her own trajectory required and rarely name as leisure. She is not lying about effort; she is misdiagnosing its source, mistaking a rare alignment of circumstances for a universal method, and hiring, without noticing, for the alignment rather than the method. This is not an argument for discarding merit as a concept; it is an argument that the belief in merit, held this innocently, becomes the mechanism by which the very advantages that produced her get quietly re-certified as qualifications. The myth does not just misdescribe the past. It manufactures the future in its own image, one hiring decision, one endowed scholarship, one grateful alumnus at a time.

Call a piece of work amateurish and you have not described it so much as sentenced it: in current usage the word does the job of a verdict — unserious, untrained, not to be admitted as evidence — and we pass it on a self-taught historian's book, a village society's excavation report, or a diagnosis offered by someone who has merely read everything on the disease. The sentence feels timeless, as though the deficiency sat in the work itself waiting for the label, and it does not feel like something with a date of manufacture.

When the word entered English in the eighteenth century, an amateur was one who pursued a thing for love, and the working contrast was not with the expert but with the mercenary; the amateur you could trust, because no salary bent his judgment. The contempt is not original to the word — it is sediment, laid down in a single and datable stratum — and the criteria by which we still convict amateur work were minted in that stratum, stamped for conditions that belonged to it. We handle the judgment daily without reading the date on the coin, and the date, once read, is the argument.

Between roughly 1870 and 1910 learning professionalized: universities began certifying training, journals installed referees, and laboratories and collections grew too costly for private means, so that by the 1890s the amateur had been redefined as a professional minus something. The new criteria — credentials, institutional affiliation, answerability to peers — were not a conspiracy; they were reasonable answers to a real problem, because serious work now required instruments only institutions could hold. In 1781 an amateur found a planet from a private garden; a century later discovery had migrated to mountaintop observatories with salaried staff, and a garden could no longer see far enough. The verdict on the amateur was, in its own era, largely a verdict on his equipment.

Whether that era's conditions still hold is the question I am declining to answer — not from delicacy, but because the evidence in hand cannot. The excavation shows the criteria were answers to a problem of access, yet it does not show what the present problem is; acquitting the amateur on the old evidence would only repeat the original error in reverse. New criteria would have to be minted before any new verdict could be read out, and no one has done the minting. Meanwhile the major sky surveys and genome consortia have committed to placing their complete archives on the open web within the decade; when those collections stand open, the question will be forced again, on workers the 1890s criteria were never cut to sort.
